To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have generated patient‐derived xenograph mouse models that recapitulate the inflammatory tumor microenvironment in PMP patients.

we have generated PDX mouse models for Pseudomyxom peritonei (a rare cancer) that recapitulate the inflammatory peritoneum microenvironment of human disease and are therefore useful in vivo surrogate models for testing and developing new therapeutic treatments for this disease.
we developed patient‐derived xenotransplantation models of PMP in immunodeficient mice and found that the inflammatory tumor microenvironment of the mouse models is similar to the human disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel treatment approaches for PMP patients.
the development of novel mouse models of PMP that are capable of recapitulating the human peritoneal tumor environment.
understanding the role of inflammation in PMP pathogenesis and the development of PDX models of PMP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PMP‐PDX mouse model is a useful model to study the inflammatory tumor microenvironment of PMP and may be useful to test novel therapies for PMP.
the PMP mouse models are a useful model to study the inflammatory peritoneum in PMP.

PMP PDX models are suitable in vivo surrogated to study the peritoneal microenviroment and tumor-stromal interactions in PMP and are useful for testing novel therapeutic interventions for PMP treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the PMP mouse models recapitulate the peritoneal microenvrionment of PMP patients and that the mouse‐derived, stromal cells are likely to be important for regulating cytokine production in the PMP microenvironment.
the PMP mouse models recapitulate the tumor microenvironment of PMP patients, which will be useful to study the pathobiology of PMP as well as to test novel therapeutic strategies.

PMP PDX models are useful for studying tumor‐stromal interaction that regulate the inflammatory peritoneum environment of PMP patients and that these mouse models are likely to be useful for developing new treatment interventions for PPM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PMP tumor‐stromal interaction is complex and the PMP PDA mouse models are useful for studying these interactions in a physiologically relevant setting.
the inflammatory tumor microenvironment in PMP is a dynamic and complex interplay between the tumor cells and tumor‐associated stromas.
PMP is not a simple mucinous adenocarcinoma.
